L80@P1: Aside from CAN’s high reliability, the main advantage of CAN over alternative networks is the low
L81@P1: development cost. CAN controller and interface cost are as low as legacy data transmission products and
L82@P1: are available off-the-shelf from leading semiconductor manufacturers. There are many CAN-related
L83@P1: system development packages, hardware interface cards, and software packages that provide system
L84@P1: designers with a wide range of design and diagnostic tools. These components provide for the
L85@P1: development of complex control applications without having to build each node of a system network.
L86@P1: Figure 1. The Layered ISO 11898:1993 Standard Architecture
L87@P1: Figure 1 displays the ISO 11898 standard architecture using the bottom two layers of the OSI model, the
L88@P1: Data-Link Layer and the Physical Layer.
L89@P1: The Data-Link Layer is responsible for transferring messages from a node to the network without errors.
L90@P1: It handles bit stuffing and checksums, and after sending a message, waits for acknowledgment from the
L91@P1: receivers.
L92@P1: The Physical Layer is the basic hardware required for a CAN network, i.e. the ISO 11898 electrical
L93@P1: specifications. It converts 1’s and 0’s into electrical pulses leaving a node, then back again for a CAN
L94@P1: message entering a node. Although the other layers may be implemented in software or in hardware as a
L95@P1: chip function, the Physical Layer is always implemented in hardware.
L96@P1: In the Figure 1 model, the Application Layer provides the upper-level communication functions of the OSI
L97@P1: layered model. These functions may be implemented by a system software developer or handled by a
L98@P1: higher-layer protocol such as the vendor-independent CANopen protocol.

L174@P2: 3 Basic Bus Communication Requirements
L175@P2: Data-Flow Model
L176@P2: Figure 2. The CAN Data-Flow Model
L177@P2: Since CAN is a broadcast system, a transmitting node places data on the network for all nodes to access.
L178@P2: As shown in Figure 2, only those nodes requiring updated data allow the message to pass through a filter
L179@P2: that is set by the network designer – i.e., messages from certain nodes can pass, and all others are
L180@P2: ignored. If this filter is not used by a system designer, much of a node's µC processing time is spent
L181@P2: sorting through messages that are not needed.
L182@P2: Every message begins with the 11-bit or 29-bit identifier shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4, that a system
L183@P2: designer can use to identify the content of a message, such as temperature or shaft position. In this way,
L184@P2: a designer can prioritize messages. For instance, an automotive message with brake information is given
L185@P2: a higher priority identifier than a turn-signal identifier. This priority is discussed in the next section.
L186@P2: Figure 3. Standard CAN: 11-Bit Identifier
L187@P2: Figure 4. Extended CAN: 29-Bit Identifier
L188@P2: CAN's multiple reception provides for the concept of modular electronics and the synchronization of
L189@P2: distributed control processes: data needed by several nodes is broadcast on the network in such a way
L190@P2: that it becomes unnecessary for a node to know origin of the data. This allows for easy servicing and
L191@P2: upgrading networks since data transmission is not dependant upon the availability of a specific type of
L192@P2: node.
L193@P2: System flexibility is achieved as a result of the content-oriented addressing scheme. This enables the
L194@P2: reconfiguration of an existing CAN network without making any hardware or software modifications. A new
L195@P2: node may be added that only receives operating data from the other transmitting nodes in a system, and
L196@P2: never sends data.
L197@P2: Note that a minimum of two nodes must be used to initialize communication on a CAN bus. Since a
L198@P2: transmitted message must be acknowledged in the ACK bit by a receiver, the transmitting controller will
L199@P2: send out an error flag if the message is not properly ACKed.

L213@P3: 4 Physical Layer Requirements
L214@P3: Physical Layer Requirements
L215@P3: All nodes on a bus participate in each bit – as it is being written. The device sending a message is also
L216@P3: receiving that message itself – checking each bit as it is written. In this way, the second node fills in the
L217@P3: ACK bit while the bit is still being transmitted by the first node. This is why it takes two nodes to complete
L218@P3: a message transmission. This function is best displayed during the arbitration shown in Figure 5. The
L219@P3: nodes of Figure 5 could theoretically be sending messages from a sensing circuit and motor controller.
L220@P3: An actual application may include a temperature sensor sending out a temperature update that is used to
L221@P3: adjust the motor speed of a fan. If a pressure sensor node wants to send a message at the same time, the
L222@P3: arbitration in Figure 5 assures that the message will be sent. On the left side of the scope Node A finishes
L223@P3: sending its message as Nodes B and C fill in the ACK bit indicating that a message is received without
L224@P3: errors. After the mandatory inter-frame space between messages, Nodes B and C then begin arbitration –
L225@P3: Node C wins the arbitration with the final dominant bit and sends its message. Nodes A and B then ACK
L226@P3: C's message. Node B then continues on with its uncontested arbitration and message which is ACKed by
L227@P3: Nodes A and C.
L228@P3: Note that if the ACK bit is missing, the transmitting controller will generate its own error flag. If a message
L229@P3: is not ACKed, an error is generated with each occurrence until the controller reaches an error limit that is
L230@P3: internally set by the CAN protocol. The controller places itself in a bus-off state when this internal limit is
L231@P3: reached. This is a protocol controller function that prevents a single node from blocking all communication
L232@P3: on a bus.
L233@P3: Figure 5. CAN Bus Traffic
L234@P3: The data link and physical signaling layers of Figure 1, which are normally transparent to a system
L235@P3: operator, are included in any controller that implements the CAN protocol such as the Texas Instruments
L236@P3: TMS320F2812™ 3.3-V DSP with integrated CAN controller. Connection to the physical medium (the bus)
L237@P3: is then implemented through a line transceiver such as TI’s SN65HVD233 3.3-V CAN transceiver to form
L238@P3: a system node shown in Figure 6.

L269@P4: 4.1 Bus Length vs Signaling Rate
L270@P4: Physical Layer Requirements
L271@P4: Figure 6. Details of a Typical CAN Node
L272@P4: The High-Speed ISO 11898 Standard specifications are given for a maximum signaling rate of 1 Mbps
L273@P4: with a bus length of 40 m and a maximum of 30 nodes. It also recommends a maximum un-terminated
L274@P4: stub length of 0.3 m. The cable is specified to be a shielded or unshielded twisted-pair with a 120-Ω
L275@P4: characteristic impedance (ZO). The Standard defines a single line of twisted-pair cable with the network
L276@P4: topology as shown in Figure 6. It is terminated at both ends with 120-Ω resistors, which match the
L277@P4: characteristic impedance of the line to prevent signal reflections. According to ISO 11898, placing RL on a
L278@P4: node should be avoided since the bus lines lose termination if the node is disconnected from the bus.
L279@P4: Table 1. Suggested Cable Length vs Signaling Rate
L280@P4: Bus Length Signaling Rate
L281@P4: (m) (Mbps)
L282@P4: 40 1
L283@P4: 100 0.5
L284@P4: 200 0.25
L285@P4: 500 0.10
L286@P4: 1000 0.05
L287@P4: Basically, the maximum bus length is determined by, or rather is a trade-off with the selected signaling
L288@P4: rate as listed in Table 1.
L289@P4: A signaling rate decreases as transmission distance increases. While steady-state losses may become a
L290@P4: factor at the longest transmission distances, the major factors limiting signaling rate as distance is
L291@P4: increased are time varying. Cable bandwidth limitations, which degrade the signal transition time and
L292@P4: introduce inter-symbol interference (ISI), are primary factors reducing the achievable signaling rate when
L293@P4: transmission distance is increased.
L294@P4: For a CAN bus, the signaling rate is also determined from the total system delay – down and back
L295@P4: between the two most distant nodes of a system and the sum of the delays into and out of the nodes on a
L296@P4: bus with the typical 5ns/m prop delay of a twisted-pair cable. Also, consideration must be given the signal
L297@P4: amplitude loss due to resistance of the cable and the input resistance of the transceivers. Under strict
L298@P4: analysis, skin effects, proximity to other circuitry, dielectric loss, and radiation loss effects all act to
L299@P4: influence the primary line parameters and degrade the signal.
L300@P4: A conservative rule of thumb for bus lengths over 100 m is derived from the product of the signaling rate
L301@P4: in Mbps and the bus length in meters, which should be less than or equal to 50.
L302@P4: Signaling Rate (Mbps) × Bus Length (m) ≤ 50

L305@P5: 4.2 Cables
L306@P5: 4.3 Shield Termination
L307@P5: 4.4 Grounding
L308@P5: 4.5 Line Terminations
L309@P5: Physical Layer Requirements
L310@P5: If a 1000 m bus is required by an application, then by this approximation a 50 kbps signaling rate may
L311@P5: safely be used. Lab experiments show that an actual safe signaling rate with 1000 m of 120-Ω
L312@P5: characteristic impedance twisted-pair cable is indeed approximately 50 kbps. By providing this extra
L313@P5: margin of safety, a lot of system variation can still take place without disruptions in communication.
L314@P5: A long cable length with a higher number of nodes than the Standard’s recommended 30 nodes may
L315@P5: require the use of higher cable quality, a CAN bus repeater, and tighter operating tolerances such as a 5%
L316@P5: voltage supply regulation. In practice, however, almost any type of cable works to a certain degree, even a
L317@P5: cheap phone line for short distances.
L318@P5: Although unshielded 120-Ω cable is used in many applications, data transmission circuits employing CAN
L319@P5: transceivers are used for jobs requiring a rugged interconnection with a wide common-mode voltage
L320@P5: range. Therefore, shielded cable such as Belden Cable 3105A is recommended in these electronically
L321@P5: harsh environments. Shielded cable and the Standard’s –2 V to 7 V common-mode range of tolerable
L322@P5: ground off-set, help to ensure data integrity. Note that the HVD1050 CAN transceiver has an extended
L323@P5: common-mode range of –12 V to 12 V.
L324@P5: While prefabricated cables for CAN applications are more expensive, they are more easily installed and
L325@P5: verified, and may, therefore, reduce overall installation cost and time-to-market.
L326@P5: If a shield must be used, it is recommended that a short pig-tail be crimped to the shield end at each
L327@P5: connector and then brought through a separate connector pin to a ground pin located as close to the
L328@P5: connector as possible. Note that the network should be grounded at a single point at the source location.
L329@P5: This prevents parasitic currents from flowing in the shield between ground connections.
L330@P5: If individual shielding of the signal pairs is used, use the same terminating technique as for the overall
L331@P5: shield.
L332@P5: There should be only one path for return current between the host and receiving nodes. This follows the
L333@P5: same discussion in the shielding section. If a network is grounded in more than one location, parasitic
L334@P5: current will flow. By grounding a network only at the source, potentially hazardous ground loops are
L335@P5: avoided. The use of digital isolators such as the ISO721 (SLLS629) is recommended if it becomes
L336@P5: necessary to connect the grounds of different sources.
L337@P5: Unused pins in connectors as well as unused wires in cables should be single-point grounded at the
L338@P5: connector. Unused wires should be grounded at alternate ends to nearby ground pins.
L339@P5: The 120-Ω characteristic impedance twisted-pair cable is terminated with an impedance of the same value
L340@P5: to minimized reflected waves that occur from miss-matched impedances. Figure 7 is an example of the
L341@P5: reflected waves that build up on a signal when termination is removed.

L369@P6: Figure 7. Unterminated and Properly Terminated Bus Signals
L370@P6: Each step in the signal is a reflected wave adding to the original signal across 1 meter of unterminated
L371@P6: twisted-pair cable. The length of each of the steps is approximately 10 ns, the typical down-and-back
L372@P6: propagation delay per meter of cable. The signal continues to build in magnitude until the supply voltage is
L373@P6: reached.
L374@P6: Two different termination models are recommended for high-speed CAN as shown in Figure 8 and
L375@P6: Figure 9. The traditional 120 Ω RL on each end of the bus, or the split termination using two 60 Ω, RL/2
L376@P6: resistors and a coupling capacitor CL. These are often used to filter high frequency components on the
L377@P6: bus.
L378@P6: Figure 8. Standard Termination
L379@P6: Care must be taken to allow for short-circuits to power supplies when selecting appropriately rated
L380@P6: termination resistors. While 1/4 W 5% tolerance resistors are generally acceptable, a bus-line short-circuit
L381@P6: to a 24 V supply line would generate a transceiver’s IOS short-circuit output current multiplied by the supply
L382@P6: voltage. The 1/4 W resistor would blow up in this circumstance.

L412@P7: Physical Layer Requirements
L413@P7: Note that transceivers such as the SN65HVD1050 have a Vref or Vsplit pin shown in Figure 9 that is
L414@P7: specifically designed to stabilize the common-mode bus voltage during communication (this also helps
L415@P7: reduce radiated emissions). The HVD1050’s Vref pin has the same wide common-mode operating range
L416@P7: and ESD protection as the bus pins.
L417@P7: Figure 10. Split Termination
L418@P7: Unwanted high frequency noise is filtered from bus lines with the split termination of Figure 10. This is
L419@P7: accomplished with coupling capacitor between two ~60 Ω ±1% termination resistors to couple high
L420@P7: frequency noise to a solid ground potential. Care must be taken to match the two resistors carefully so as
L421@P7: to not reduce the effective immunity. This technique improves the electromagnetic compatibility of a
L422@P7: network. A typical value of CL for a high-speed CAN is 4.7 nF, which generates a 3 dB point at 1.1 Mbps.
L423@P7: This, of course is a signaling rate dependant value.
L424@P7: Connectors, while not specified by the Standard, should have a characteristic impedance matching that of
L425@P7: the bus line and terminators, and it should not affect standard operating parameters such as the minimum
L426@P7: VOD.
L427@P7: The higher layer protocols such as CANopen and DeviceNet define the specific hardware required for
L428@P7: implementation, including bus wire and connectors. Recommended products may be found on
L429@P7: organization web-sites such as the CiA’s CAN-cia.com which list connector and pin-out specifications for
L430@P7: use in CANopen applications. These include the 9-pin DSUB shown in Figure 11, Multipole, RJ10, RJ45,
L431@P7: M12, the 5-pin mini-style in Figure 12 and more micro-style connectors in the CiA specification document
L432@P7: DR 303-1, V1-3.

L459@P8: Bus-lines and a ground plane can form a loop for inductively coupled noise signals and depending upon
L460@P8: the topology, a bus can easily become an antenna for local noise.
L461@P8: Figure 13. Coupled Noise
L462@P8: The cables used in Figure 13 are different lengths of unshielded twisted-pair 24 AWG copper wire and the
L463@P8: figure clearly displays the inducted noise from nearby florescent lighting. Properly filtered, these would be
L464@P8: four noise-free straight lines. Induced voltages of 10 V or more are commonly found on industrial buses.
L465@P8: Chokes such as the ZJYS81RS-2PL51(T)-G01 have been developed by TDK specifically to address this
L466@P8: problem in CAN applications.
L467@P8: Since stub-lines are unterminated, signal reflections can develop in a stub that drive signal levels back
L468@P8: and forth across a receiver's input thresholds, creating errors. Bit-sampling occurs near the end of a bit, so
L469@P8: it is mandatory that all signal reflections in a CAN stub-line be attenuated before or during the propagation
L470@P8: delay segment in Figure 15 to provide an adequate margin of safety.
L471@P8: To minimized reflections, stub-line length should not exceed one-third (1/3) of the line's critical length.
L472@P8: Beyond this stub-length, many variables come into play since the stub is no longer considered to be a
L473@P8: lumped parameter. This is the maximum length that a stub remains invisible to a transmission line.
L474@P8: The critical length of a bus line occurs at the point where the down-and-back propagation delay
L475@P8: (tprop(total)) of a signal through a line equals the transition time(t
L476@P8: t) of a signal (the greater of the rise or fall
L477@P8: times).
L478@P8: Network Critical Length = t
L479@P8: t = tprop(total)
L480@P8: Therefore, a typical CAN driver may have a 50 ns transition time, and when considering a typical
L481@P8: twisted-pair transmission line prop delay of 5 ns/m, the down-and-back delay for one meter becomes
L482@P8: 10ns/m. The critical length becomes 5 m (50 ns / 10ns/m = 5 m), and the max un-terminated stub length
L483@P8: for the network is 1/3rdof the critical length, or 5/3 m (1.67 m).
